General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

The Golden Rules of Affordable Family Travel, Illustrated by Mona Chalabi

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2245 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • My first Thanksgiving was a lavish 12-person dinner in Connecticut in 2014.
  • Take it from an immigrant: this holiday is full of weird contradictions.
  • As we approach the last Thursday of November, with money very much on our minds, the below well-traveled parents share their hard-won wisdom on pulling off affordable family travel—including how to find treasure in New York City’s Chinatown without paying an arm and a leg, seek out free entertainment in the streets of Oaxaca, and embrace the joys of accessible public transportation in Europe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

My first Thanksgiving was a lavish 12-person dinner in Connecticut in 2014. I had moved to the US in March of that year and had planned on working from home until a friend generously invited me to go spend the day with her family; an act of unguarded openness that I’ve realized is one of the many things that differentiates Americans from Brits. As soon as we got off the train in Cambridge, Massachusetts, I realized that even though my friend lived in a nasty, overcrowded apartment in Brooklyn, she came from a family that had immense wealth. After dinner, as I helped wash plates in the kitchen, my friend’s mum asked her why she wouldn’t just move into the lovely building they had bought for her. She turned beet red and handed me another dirty plate without looking at me.

Take it from an immigrant: this holiday is full of weird contradictions. Of course, there’s the annual reminder of colonization which requires a careful forgetting of the people who have been colonized. And then there’s the financial aspect of it. At first blush, it seems like the least capitalist holiday of the year—there isn’t the expense of Christmas or Hanukkah gift-giving or the extravagance of Halloween candy. Yet the holiday also marks the start of one of the year's busiest travel seasons when families are taking great expense to reunite, vacation, and explore outside of their every day lives.

As we approach the last Thursday of November, with money very much on our minds, the below well-traveled parents share their hard-won wisdom on pulling off affordable family travel—including how to find treasure in New York City’s Chinatown without paying an arm and a leg, seek out free entertainment in the streets of Oaxaca, and embrace the joys of accessible public transportation in Europe. All of these stories say something about the wealth of the person writing it, whether or not they wanted to reveal that information. I’m obsessed with getting to the truth about someone’s class (it’s why I wrote my book on the subject), and so these family dispatches, which serve as equal parts advice and confession, are a treat I’ll come back to when I’m not busy washing a rich family’s plates. —Mona Chalabi, Pulitzer Prize-winning writer and illustrator.

Keep reading for the tips and tricks of affordable family travel, road-tested by the experts and illustrated by Mona Chalabi.

I know the secret to parenting and I’m willing to share it: snacks. Snacks are everything—they’re an activity, a mood changer, and a window into culture for kids. Hit a local farmers market on your first day or if you’re somewhere truly out of their comfort zone even a local convenience store—like 7-Eleven in Tokyo—for something that can feel both familiar and novel. If your hotel room has a refrigerator you can store any pre-cut fruit that you buy, or opt for items that don’t require refrigeration like apples, bananas, and clementines. Bring a lightweight backpack, refill each morning, and watch the hangry meltdowns (mostly) vanish. —Dana Kravis, global executive director, CNT video.

Sources indicate that last December in London, we stayed in a quaint Airbnb in Primrose Hill and explored different neighborhoods on foot. When our kids, then eight and three, got tired, we hopped on a double-decker bus and headed upstairs, hoping for front seats. Suddenly, getting home became an amusement park ride: Christmas lights, bustling streets, panoramic views. The kids loved it; as a photographer, I loved the vantage point. London caps daily bus fares when you use the same card or phone, and children under 11 ride free. We’ve done this in Singapore, too. Our rule: skip the sightseeing tour (or Uber) and make public transportation part of the family adventure. —Tanveer Badal, photographer.

Breakfast is where family vacations are made, or broken. My moody teenagers can’t be pried out of bed no matter what city they wake up in, so instead of wringing my uncaffeinated hands and hoping to get us all on the same schedule, I just bring my own breakfast, coffee included. Whether in Paris, Rome, or a tent, you will find me hand-grinding my coffee beans, brewing a pour-over, and snacking on a pastry left over from the previous day while I peruse headlines. Avoiding the time and expense of a sit-down breakfast, and indulging in a bit of morning self-care, means we can focus on the adventures and meals we are actually going to remember. —Chris Morocco, food director of Bon Appétit and Epicurious.

In a recent development, my parents and I meet in Aruba every winter for a family vacation that’s warm and relaxing when everyone else is cold and miserable. It’s a classic only child/parents trip where we spend most of our time eating lunch talking about where we’re going to eat dinner. We spend our days mostly just reading parallel to each other. I’ve never been an e-reader user, so I have to bring several physical books to read to get me through the week. The key is that my mom and I have some shared taste in books, so when we finish our own we can swap and save ourselves buying extra books (or lugging even heavier luggage through the airport). —Alison Leiby, comedian and writer.

It has been revealed that finding creative ways to entertain wiggly one-year-olds with limited attention spans can be daunting, but it turns out all you need is a good window. From London to California, staying in rooms on low floors with windows overlooking lots of activity below has resulted in seemingly endless engagement—waving at commuters striding by or golfers strolling a few feet away? Bonus points if the room has curtains with electronic controls—that guarantees an extra hour of ooohs and aaahs, at least. —Sarah Khan, contributing editor.

I have a thing for seeing “The World’s Biggest or Oldest,” and so here we were at Missouri’s Oldest Wooden Suspension Bridge. “Don’t tell your mom,” I stated to my kids, because any bridge that was built from wood during the Civil War should be treated with caution—and, also, all good dad stories start that way. We started up the van, piled everyone in, and began the adventure. The wood cracked and echoed as we drove over the river. It sounded like a popping spinal cord. We swayed, and for a moment, I actually questioned myself. I should have just taken them to the park. Thankfully, I can now confidently say that Missouri’s oldest wooden suspension bridge can hold the weight of a mini-van. —Shannon Carpenter, humorist.

Industry observers note that latest York is an expensive city and the best way to keep it cheap is to throw petty cash at it. Instead of buying tickets to an overpriced kid’s experience, I give my children a few twenty dollar bills and take them to Chinatown for a shopping spree. They love the atrocious arcade, and there are fake Labubus, squishy dumplings, a plastic “jade” green dragon that my son now keeps on his bedside, and a 'gold' necklace my daughter thinks is treasure. —Stephanie Danler, author.

As a seasoned travel writer, I know that any hotel that’s gotten media coverage is often pushing $1,000/night. My trick for affordable family lodging is loading up Google maps, figuring out which area we’re going to stay in, and picking a cheerful place with good reviews in the $250 range. It’s almost never one you’ve heard of, but they’re always clean and cheerful, usually family-owned, and we always leave with massive hugs and promises to keep in touch. That doesn’t happen at the Georges V. My kids (12 and 8) loved a converted windmill in Rome, a townhouse two blocks from the Rijksmuseum and—most recently—an orange grove near Siracusa where they spent so much time chasing the owner’s cats they even forgot Wi-Fi existed. A steal at any price! —Priyanka Mattoo, filmmaker and author.

Recent findings suggest that people tell you about a million things you “need” before your baby is born, but there's one that has come in the most handy, and I've had a true love/hate relationship with it since day one: A travel car seat. After a ton of research—some may say over-research—we bought a Maxi Cosi Romi. It's rated high for safety, but it's also easy to strap into a car and also an airplane. We always bring it on the airplane, and that's where the headache comes in. While the Maxi Cosi Romi is considered lightweight, it's also big and bulky, and the only way to get it through the airport and onto the plane is by wearing it in a special backpack. I'm pretty sure that I'm one of the most annoying people in any airport as I'm walking through it since I can't really see if I'm bumping into people in the TSA line or getting to the gate. The thing is that, after I considered the numbers, it's actually a really wise investment because most rental car places charge anywhere from $10 to $15 a day to rent a car seat, so we've already started saving money because of it. Now, that's about a hundred or more dollars we're not spending when we go out of town and bring the Maxi. It's wildly annoying and inconvenient, and I look like I'm wearing a jetpack as I'm walking through the airport, but it's worth it. —Jason Diamond, 'Figuring' family columnist at The Cut.

Recent findings suggest that I️ live in Brooklyn where people leave really good stuff out on the street. Once I️ found one of those giant extra storage containers you put on top of your car. I️ haven't found the time to figure out how to put it on top of the car; it's been taking up valuable space in my home for over a year. The other day, I️ found another one that looked even fancier. I️ dragged it home. One day, ideally before our car gets too old to work anymore, I️ will figure this out, then get rid of the extra one somehow (do I️ need to call 311?). After that, my husband, our two kids, our dog, our parakeets and I️ will pack up everything we could possibly need to rent a house somewhere for a week or two. I️ have my eye on Block Island or Martha's Vineyard. —Liana Finck, cartoonist and author.

From bustling markets to neighborhood festivals, I've learned that some of the best family entertainment happens in the streets. In Oaxaca, my four-year-old was mesmerized by calendas, raucous community processions with brass bands, towering puppets called monos de calenda, and rag-covered revelers known as tiliches. Paradegoers tossed my kid candy, fireworks exploded overhead, and the party raged late into the night. We didn't pay a peso. Before booking pricey family activities, research local festivals, celebrations, and public performances. Sometimes the most exciting show in town is happening right on the sidewalk. —Ashlea Halpern, contributing editor.

On our last family vacation to Rajasthan, a passionfruit lassi from our five-star hotel nearly ruined the trip. We’re talking emergency roadside bathroom stops and several days of Zofran. We’ve been taking our kids—Vijay, Vik, and Meera—to Rajasthan since they were babies; they’re teenagers now. And we’ve learned one unexpected lesson: the sickest we’ve ever been in India was after eating at our five-star hotel. More than once.

So we’ve adopted a fresh philosophy: pack the right medicine and embrace street food. In Jaipur, Vineet Sharma, founder of Jaipur Walks, led us on a street food tour around the bustling market, introducing us to piping-hot pyaaz kachori and creamy, saffron-rich kulfi. His advice? Choose clean stalls with high turnover, and favor food cooked fresh and served hot over raw offerings. At busy stalls, food is often prepared continuously and served straight from the heat—sometimes a more reassuring bet than a meal at a luxury hotel or high-end restaurant. And if your stomach’s going to revolt, at least make the meal memorable. —Christine Chitnis, author and photographer.

Industry observers note that this may not be the most popular piece of advice, and I doubt it'll be the most obvious: take your kids overseas during school time. Hear me out: the longer you can stretch your child's travels beyond the limited school holidays when ticket prices always soar, the better for your wallet. Of course, every parent needs to set their own boundary on what and how much school their kind can miss in the name of travel but I feel, especially at a young age, the benefits of the trip outweigh the additional days in the classroom. As I am writing this, I am preparing to leave tomorrow with my first grader for Italy for a week. We are cooking up aims to take our two kids on a long haul trip to the southern hemisphere that'll cut into a week of school. I have heard from more than one expert that Disney especially, should be done when your kids are young, and outside normal school holidays if you want to get great value. I don't do it often but I do balance the guilt with rules—we have to read every day, and do exercises from a homework packet to keep on top of the basics. One day, and soon, I know I won't want to do this much more. But for now, I'm taking every chance to do so. —Erin Florio, global features director.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Transcend Cruises has launched a partnership with Your Health Companion (YHC) to introduce a personal health benefit designed to enhance the well-being, confidence and peace of mind of its charter river cruise guests.

“At Transcend Cruises, we are continually looking for innovative ways to elevate the guest experience. Our partnership with Your Health Companion reflects our commitment to providing guests not only with extraordinary travel experiences but also with greater confidence and peace of mind while exploring the world,” stated Edie Rodriguez, CEO, Transcend Cruises.

Through this partnership, Transcend Cruises guests will receive complimentary seven-day access to Your Health Companion, a personal health management app that puts essential medical information, health resources and AI-powered symptom guidance directly at their fingertips.

After the complimentary period, guests who want to keep enjoying the app’s comprehensive features can purchase an annual subscription at a reduced price, extending these benefits beyond their river cruise and into their everyday lives.

Transcend said in a press release that Your Health Companion helps guests access the informational and organizational benefits of having their doctor’s office in their pocket, available directly from their smartphone wherever internet connectivity is available.

“We believe that traveling away from home should never mean being disconnected from your personal health information,” remarked Scott Grody, CEO, Your Health Companion.

“Our partnership with Transcend Cruises represents an exciting advancement in bringing personalized health technology to the travel industry. We are providing travelers with many of the benefits of having their doctor’s office in their pocket, wherever their journey takes them,” added Grody.

Jeffries puts immigration bill high on Democratic priority list

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (731 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., holds a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday.
  • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move rapidly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.
  • Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., holds a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move rapidly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.

Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.

“One of the things that we need to do is to move the Dream and Promise Act for DACA recipients and TPS recipients,” Jeffries said, referring to a Democratic bill introduced last year. “We should actually move that bill immediately.”.

Industry observers note that the proposal aims to create a path to citizenship for certain Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals recipients and Temporary Protected Status holders. Similar legislation has been a top priority for Democrats in both chambers for more than a decade, with Democrats unable to advance this bill in the House while Republicans have held the majority.

Jeffries also reiterated his calls to rein in Immigration and Customs Enforcement and redirect funding allocated to the agency through Republicans' budget law known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, while expressing a desire for bipartisan cooperation on immigration more broadly.

In a recent development, “We think the border should be safe and strong and secure, and we think our immigration system overall is broken,” Jeffries noted. “We need to fix it in a comprehensive way, and certainly, it's our hope that a handful of Republicans will be willing to join us, so we can fix it in a bipartisan way.”.

On healthcare, however, Jeffries offered fewer specifics, suggesting Democrats still have decisions to make before taking control of the chamber. Democrats broadly agree on the need to restore subsidies for prepares purchased through health insurance markets that expired at the end of 2025. But the question of what additional steps the party should pursue with the goal of expanding coverage and lowering prices is likely to be a major test of Democratic leadership’s ability to find consensus among its robust newly introduced majority.

When asked how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that's all part of an ongoing conversation.”.

The New York Democrat outlined several broader healthcare priorities, including reversing Medicaid cuts enacted under President Donald Trump, extending Affordable Care Act tax credits, all of which Democrats have vowed to do over the last year.

“Out of the gate, what we clearly have to do is fix our broken healthcare system in terms of the damage that's been done by Donald Trump and MAGA extremists over the last two years, and that clearly involves reversing the Medicaid cuts and extending the Affordable Care Act tax credits, and beginning to engage in supporting medical research, particularly things like research for pediatric cancer,” Jeffries added.

Democrats established a healthcare working group earlier this Congress, led by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. and Terri Sewell, D-Ala., to gather perspectives and develop policy proposals as the party works toward a broader agenda.

Recent findings suggest that without an unveiled challenger, Jeffries has expressed confidence that he’ll secure the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who have mentioned they remain “undecided” ahead of Wednesday’s elections. Jeffries, who was introduced as “Speaker Jeffries” on election night, said last week he was “very confident we’ll get there” and confirmed that the caucus will hold a recorded vote in the contest.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to go forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives, many aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America, had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

Jeffries noted Tuesday the approach mirrors the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who is best positioned to lead based on “track record, experience and vision.”.

This report was corrected to reflect Rep. Nancy Pelosi’s status as a current member.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Speaking during the delivery of the MSC World Asia in Saint-Nazaire on Wednesday, Chantiers de l’Atlantique General Manager Laurent Castaing highlighted the vessel’s energy efficiency and celebrated the shipyard’s 25-year partnership with MSC Cruises.

The handover marks the 20th cruise ship built by the French yard for the manufacturer, adding a upcoming vessel to the World Class series, which began in 2022 with the MSC World Europa.

“This ship is exceptional,” Castaing stated. “Following the wishes of her shipowner and thanks to our great flexibility, major new features for passengers have been added to this excellent World Class platform.”.

He also pointed to the sustainability features of the vessel, noting that its greenhouse gas emissions are 50 percent lower than the IMO reference baseline.

Industry observers note that “What we are very proud of is the environmental performance of this ship. From a distance, she looks like others, but she is truly exceptional, and we have extensively modified the ship’s machinery,” Castaing noted.

“She is the best in energy efficiency across the entire cruise ship fleet, and by far. Few modes of transport can boast such a 50 percent reduction compared to the benchmarks. We are ahead of our competitors, and we will continue moving toward zero emissions.”.

Castaing said the ship was the result of human effort, adding that thousands of people had worked on its construction since 2024.

He thanked MSC Cruises for the partnership with Chantiers de l’Atlantique, noting that the tech giant has now built 20 ships at the French yard over the past 25 years.

Recent findings suggest that “It is exceptional. Our relationship has always been one of trust. We have not weathered any storms in our relations. Sometimes clouds have passed by, but honestly, I have never gone to Geneva with a knot in my stomach,” Castaing said.

“Even if there were occasionally a few last-minute squabbles, our deliveries have always gone smoothly and have always been celebrated with dignity here in Saint-Nazaire, just like today, and we thank you for that,” he mentioned, addressing MSC Cruises Executive Chairman Pierfrancesco Vago.

Castaing said that MSC Cruises has brought more than 100 million hours of work to Chantiers de l’Atlantique over 25 years.

“Building ships is not only about relationships between people, even though that matters enormously. There are also tens of billions of euros in orders, tens of billions of euros necessary for our trade balance,” he added.

Senators still see NDAA as chance for online safety legislation

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (680 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday.
  • Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.
  • Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.

Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.

It has been revealed that the Senate Judiciary Committee’s panel on Crime and Counterterrorism held the hearing after its Chairman Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and ranking member Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., introduced a bill Monday that would ban pre-dispute arbitration agreements from affecting cases where a minor was harmed online, including by sexual exploitation.

Hawley and Durbin also worked together on a separate bill to expand eligibility for victims of abuse to bring civil suits against online platforms that intentionally, knowingly or recklessly promoted or facilitated the abuse. It would also include penalties for certain platforms that fail to report child pornography violations on their sites.

Industry observers note that that bill is included in a manager’s amendment to the Senate’s fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill. Durbin encouraged Congress to pass the NDAA “in the closing days” of the session because “protecting children is an notable part of it.”.

In a recent development, “I have a few weeks left in my service in the United States Senate,” said Durbin, who is retiring at the end of his term in January. “I’m thinking each day it’s coming to an end, but I want it to come [to an] end the right way.”.

The subcommittee has spent much of the 119th Congress focused on harms to children online, including from artificial intelligence chatbots.

Tuesday’s hearing included testimony from survivors and experts on child exploitation on Roblox.

Hawley said that victims are bound by pre-dispute agreements with Roblox to settle claims through private arbitration, rather than in court.

Recent findings suggest that “They slam the courthouse door shut in their faces,” Hawley said. “We’re talking about children now, child victims of sexual exploitation online are denied their day in court by the very company that has exposed them to the content to begin with.”.

A spokesperson for Roblox said in a statement that “safety has been central” to the platform since its launch.

Industry observers note that “We require age checks for chat, place users under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” the spokesperson said. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a company’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”.

According to recent reports, myriam Gilles, a professor of law at Northwestern University, told the panel that a 2022 law that ended forced arbitration agreements for victims of sexual assault has gaps. She noted Roblox has argued it does not apply to online actions, just “completed physical assault” and does not apply to platforms.

She also remarked that Hawley’s fresh arbitration bill would enhance the effects of his measure regarding civil suits by making sure those suits can be heard publicly if families so choose.

“Congress can pass laws, but if [suits] just get shunted into private arbitration, they’re doing no good in the world,” Gilles remarked. “A right to sue that ends in secret arbitration is a right in name only.”.

The hearing came the same day that advocates, including reality TV personality and activist Paris Hilton, held a press conference to urge House action on a bill (S 1837) that would allow individuals to bring civil suits over nonconsensual intimate depictions generated by artificial intelligence or for possession or production of deepfake porn if there was also intent to disclose the images.

That bill passed the Senate in January but has not been taken up in the House.

Latest Update: How I Got My Visa to France

📅 16 Feb 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1976 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nomadicmatt

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’ve been in love with France ever since my first trip to Bordeaux in 2010.
  • Recent findings suggest that but that love became an obsession when, after Bordeaux, I stepped out of the Paris metro and onto the Champs-Élysées.
  • Since then, Paris has had a firm grip on my heart.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve been in love with France ever since my first trip to Bordeaux in 2010. Friends I had met back in Thailand indicated me around the area and introduced me to French culture. It was my first time in France and I loved the food, the wine, and the people.

Recent findings suggest that but that love became an obsession when, after Bordeaux, I stepped out of the Paris metro and onto the Champs-Élysées. The lights, the energy, the mystique! There was magic in the air. I felt like I had known the city my entire life and I was simply returning home.

Since then, Paris has had a firm grip on my heart. Over the years, I spent countless visits exploring France and Paris in particular. I’ve run tours in the city and I spent a few months living there in 2019.

Last August, after yet another sojourn, I thought to myself, “What if I moved back?”.

I was growing a bit tired of the NYC dating scene, the rising cost of living, and felt like, creatively, I was in a rut. With AI coming for creators like me and the industry changing, I was a little lost on what, career-wise, would come next.

And Paris seemed like the best place to go.

It’s cheaper than NYC, I had friends there already, I’ve always wanted to learn French, it would make a great base for exploring Europe, and I could start writing my next book there. There’s nothing like a change in scenery to get the creativity flowing!

But the question remained: how do you move to France?

After all, they don’t have a digital nomad visa, and you’re limited to three months if you visit on your regular Schengen tourist visa.

It has been revealed that well, it turns out that it’s not actually that hard. (And while I can only speak for Americans, I suspect the criteria are similar for Canadians, Aussies, Kiwis, and other “developed” nations.).

If you want to move to France, you have four main options:.

The student visa is pretty straightforward. You need to enroll in a full-time university program and show you have enough funds to support yourself (around 600 Euros per month). A friend is currently there on this visa, as she is doing a nine-month intensive French program to become fluent. You still have to apply for the visa, but if you’re enrolled in an accredited school, you’ll likely get approved. Another benefit to this visa is that you can work part-time on it!

In a recent development, but this visa is contingent on being in school, so if you leave or quit, it’s voided. However, when you are done, you can change this to a “job seeker” visa, which can give you up to another six months in France (or more depending on how long your program was).

I thought about applying for the entrepreneur visa, but the application process is pretty complex and can take months to be approved. You have to set up your business in France — and that is a lot of paperwork. You have to show that your business makes money, has clients (at least one of them being French), and can support you full-time (you have to make at least the French minimum wage). They will scrutinize your assets and financials a lot and you’ll need to register your business in France and pay French taxes.

In a recent development, additionally, France offers a talent visa. If you’re an expert in your field (with verifiable accreditations and accolades), this could be a good visa to apply for, especially if you plan to stay in France for a long time and want to physically work there. But, again, you’ll need to have some source of income and plan to do physical business in France. If you’re not an academic but someone in the arts, you have to show how you are going to add to the “culture of France” in some way.

While I would meet the requirements for both those visas, the process for either would have been time-consuming, and, since I’m not sure France is going to be my forever home, I decided not to go through that process.

So I went with the long-term visitor visa, officially called VLS-TS visiteur. This allows me to stay up to 12 months in France and is renewable in the country. It does come with a lot of restrictions, however: I can’t physically work here and I am not allowed into the French social welfare system.

It’s also the visa a lot of Americans (and most retirees) are coming in on. If you have passive income or retirement savings and just want to live in France, this is a good option for you. It allows you to set up a bank account and it can be renewed pretty much indefinitely.

It has been revealed that the paperwork for this visa (which I’ll get into in a bit) essentially comes down to whether or not you can support yourself. French authorities want to make sure you won’t be a burden on the system.

My biggest question centered around whether or not I could “work” on this visa. A lot of creators and digital nomads are applying for — and getting — this visa.

But remember: you aren’t allowed to work on this visa so how are you going to work if you can’t work?

So let me take a moment to talk about “work” from a legal standpoint.

It has been revealed that as I mentioned, there’s no digital nomad visa that allows you to work in France. And the French tax office said last July that remote work is considered taxable — but there are no official laws that say so. That’s just their opinion and there’s been no progress in codifying that opinion. In fact, my visa doesn’t even come with a tax number, so I can’t be taxed. I couldn’t pay taxes even if I wanted to.

The visa office asks how you’ll support yourself when you are in France and one of the sources of income they accept is “income from work.” I was very open that my means of support would be the income from this blog and my books.

The system there really hasn’t caught up to remote work. It still defines “work” as something you do physically that could take away a job from a French person.

According to recent reports, so could I run walking tours in Paris? Nope. Could you work at a café? Nope.

But does writing this blog post count as work? After all, no one is paying for it. It’s a free resource. Does going to a café to work on the next great American novel count? What about my weekly newsletter that has affiliate links (that generate income) in it? Is writing that considered work?

Recent findings suggest that the gray area is considerable, so the best thing to do is to talk to a lawyer. I recommend Daniel Tostado (yes, that’s his real name), one of the biggest American-French immigration lawyers in Paris. He has a huge law firm and regularly meets with government officials to clarify the rules on this. He gave me some solid advice.

Industry observers note that for this long-term visitor visa, the application process is pretty easy. You go to the French government website, fill out your application, take the application number to the TLScontact website, and make an appointment. (France outsources the appointment process to this company, which then sends everything to the French consulate for approval.).

The main things you’ll want to demonstrate are that you have accommodation for 90 days on your application and enough income to support yourself. They just want to make sure you aren’t going to be a burden on the system. I went overboard. Here’s what I brought to my appointment:.

I didn’t need the second bank account, tax returns, or W-2 (they weren’t required) but the woman at the appointment mentioned the more proof you had the better and it wouldn’t hurt. And another friend who got this visa didn’t bring anything beyond what was asked in the application form. But I wanted to take no chances!

Sources indicate that at the appointment, the staff double-checks your paperwork, takes your biometric data, collects the fees, and then sends your passport to the embassy for processing. Officially, it takes up to 15 days to process your visa, but everyone I know seems to get it back within a week.

The worst part was not knowing if you are approved until your passport is returned. While you can track the progress of your application, you don’t know the verdict until your passport is back in your hands. While I was waiting (and anxiously spiraling), I looked on Reddit and found that most denials were for lack of income or issues with their accommodation, which seem to be the two most key things to have perfect on your application.

It has been revealed that once you get your visa back, you can enter France any time after the start date. After you enter, you have 90 days to register your visa with the state (they give you a little QR code with instructions). This allows you to “officially” be on this long-term visa. (It’s a more paperwork kind of thing.).

Once that is done, there’s nothing else to do and you can stay in France (and Europe) until your visa expires!

According to recent reports, so, if you’re considering moving to France, these are your options. But, as always, I’m not a lawyer and this is not legal advice. In regard to work and other issues or questions, it’s important that you seek legal counsel and get their expert opinion!

Tech Report: Don’t Visit Ko Lipe

📅 23 Feb 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1265 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nomadicmatt

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, after 19 years, I finally went back to Ko Lipe, the Thai island I spent close to a month on in 2006.
  • It has been revealed that there was much to do here but that was the point.
  • Industry observers note that it was paradise – and a place a lot of people got stuck.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, after 19 years, I finally went back to Ko Lipe, the Thai island I spent close to a month on in 2006. Back then, it was one of those super off-the-beaten-path destinations that few but the most intrepid travelers visited, where electricity only ran a few hours a day, basic bungalows right on the beach cost something like $2 USD, and there really was a last boat for the season.

It has been revealed that there was much to do here but that was the point. You hung out on the beach, read a book, went snorkeling, went back to the beach, drank beers at the one beach bar on the island, rotated meals between the five restaurants there, and went to bed early.

Industry observers note that it was paradise – and a place a lot of people got stuck. Days easily turned into weeks here.

Recent findings suggest that if you asked me what the highlight of all my travels was, I would be the time I spent on Ko Lipe. I made incredible friends, lounged around, got to know the locals, learned a bit of Thai, and, overall, lived that idyllic backpacker life we all dream about.

Recent findings suggest that over the years, I’ve avoided going back to Ko Lipe because the memory of my time there is so strong that I didn’t want to ruin it. Any re-visit would simply be trying to recreated a magic that couldn’t be recreated because the people that it special wouldn’t be there. I’d be chasing travel ghosts. And, since I know my sleepy paradise has been developed greatly over the years, I was also too afraid seeing that would make me sad.

Tourism in Thailand tends toward the unsustainable. No island really develops in a good way. It’s all build, build, build.

And I didn’t want to see my Ko Lipe like that.

But as I was planning my recent trip through Southeast Asia, returning to Ko Lipe made sense. I was heading down the Indian Ocean side of Thailand on my way into Malaysia and I’d pass by it.

Sources indicate that and, since I was looking for a lively place for New Year’s Eve, it seemed liked the best choice. I knew there would be travelers there and there were no other nearby islands that would work, especially since Ko Lipe has a boat to Langkawi, which was my next stop.

And I’m sad to report that Ko Lipe took the Ko Phi Phi model of tourism and is now extremely overdeveloped.

Most of the island is now paved over, the old dirt footpaths having become concrete for the cars and construction trucks. Swaths of palm trees are now the sites of high-end resorts with pools (on an island with no natural water supply). Construction of more resorts continues at a fast pace. The coral around the island is dying, a victim of all the boats, anchors, pollution, and overfishing. Beaches are now lined with boats, their exhaust spilling into the ocean, leaving a shiny film you can see as you swim. And the restaurants cater to tourists looking for bad Western food, not great Thai cuisine.

Sources indicate that the island’s boom has displaced many locals, who were forced to sell to mainland developers, and much of the island’s workforce is now from the mainland. They see little of the benefits this tourism boom.

So lies Ko Lipe, another victim of Thailand’s all too common overdevelopment and exploitation of limited resources.

I met lots of people there who loved the island. If it’s your first time, I can see why you would love it. After all, the area is postcard perfect, the water is perfectly an azure blue, the sand is a beautiful white, and since you’re surrounded by a national park, a lot of tours take you to some secluded islands.

And, in comparison to Ko Phi Phi, Krabi, or Phuket, it is less developed so I can’t fault someone stepping here for the first time going “wow!”.

But, as I reflect on the island and its overdevelopment, I have come to the same conclusion I have about Ko Phi Phi: people shouldn’t visit.

I’m not against growth, but I’m against this kind of growth. It’s not sustainably managed and going there will only tax the island’s limited resources even further. You can’t put the genie back in the bottle and no local is going to say “sure, I’ll stay broke so you can an idealized vision of the world.”.

And, with so many other islands to visit that are well managed (Ko Lanta, Ko Jum, and Ko Mook, to name three nearby), I think you should skip Ko Lipe.

A visit there will only make things worse.

Recent findings suggest that it pains me to say that, because it was such a beautiful place, and my original visit had a huge impact on my life. But if we’re going to be good stewards and travelers, sometimes you just have to say enough is enough.

And Ko Lipe is a place where enough is enough.

Go somewhere else that is better managed.

Because your choices do have an impact.

According to recent reports, riding elephants in Thailand went away when consumers became more conscious of it. Eco lodges got big because of consumers. Overtourism is talked about by consumers as much as it is by locals.

Maybe if enough people start to do something, Ko Lipe will change.

But, at the very least, by not going you are at least no contributing to the problem.

Charlotte Amalie Harbor Dredging to Start This Week

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (347 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Cruiseindustrynews

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that dredging activity for the Charlotte Amalie Harbor project in St.
  • According to VIPA Executive Director Ava Penn, mobilization is underway and the dredging activity is scheduled to start by Friday, November 27, 2026.
  • The project involves dredging the harbor’s entrance channel, turning basin and West Indian Company Limited (WICO) berthing pocket in Havensight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that dredging activity for the Charlotte Amalie Harbor project in St. Thomas is set to start this week, Virgin Islands Port Authority (VIPA) shared in a press release.

According to VIPA Executive Director Ava Penn, mobilization is underway and the dredging activity is scheduled to start by Friday, November 27, 2026.

The project involves dredging the harbor’s entrance channel, turning basin and West Indian Company Limited (WICO) berthing pocket in Havensight.

The multimillion-dollar maritime infrastructure investment is expected to improve navigational access to the Charlotte Amalie Harbor, accommodate the evolving needs of the cruise industry and strengthen the U.S. Virgin Islands’ position as a Caribbean cruise destination.

The dredging project will be conducted in two phases.

Phase 1 — Nov. 2026 through March 2027: This phase will consist of dredging the non-beach quality material from the entrance channel, turning basin and WICO berth pocket.

Phase 2 — March 2027 through October 2027: This phase will consist of dredging the beach-quality material from the entrance channel.

Dredging activities will be conducted seven days a week, Main Channel and Turning Basin from sunrise to sunset, and overnight for WICO Berthing Pocket and Bulkhead.

Preparations are underway on both St. Croix and St. Thomas, both of which welcomed the barges, dredge and survey vessels supporting the project.

Industry observers note that at St. Croix, preparation of the temporary stockpile site, including clearing and grubbing activities, has started, with fences installed and stabilized entrances to the site constructed. Preparation of the designated quarry site will follow completion of the temporary stockpile site.

On St. Thomas, a pre-dredging survey of Charlotte Amalie Harbor was conducted to establish the existing harbor conditions and assist with monitoring the dredging work.

It has been revealed that VIPA said that its contractor cleared most of the former Addelita Cancryn Junior High School property located in Crown Bay, St. Thomas, and will use the property for dredged material storage.

Demolition of the buildings on the site started in June 2026.

#214633. Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1010 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1010 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday.
  • Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s new ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.
  • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s new ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.

The original ask contained roughly $12 billion that was tied directly to air traffic control upgrades, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said, with the remainder going toward long-sought airport terminal and other upgrades to aging aviation facilities.

Duffy and Vought laid out in a letter to House and Senate appropriators on Tuesday what the extra $20 billion would be for — half for construction of five newly introduced air route traffic control centers, and half for construction, replacement and improvement of up to 140 air traffic control towers.

They justified the increased demand because of the “urgent need” that became evident after the ground stop. Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford fanned out across the Capitol to try to sell the request, including a stop at Senate Republicans’ weekly policy lunch.

But it quickly became evident that their own allies on Capitol Hill want more and better justification for why so much extra money is needed.

Not only are there concerns that much of the request would go to terminal reconstruction and other longer-term projects, but lawmakers keep noting the FAA hasn’t yet spent about $8 billion out of the initial $12.5 billion “down payment” on air traffic control modernization provided in last year’s budget reconciliation law.

“I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded,” Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday. “What we just discussed there, and what I expressed, is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.”.

Still, Cruz stated the administration had done a “good job” with the initial $12.5 billion modernization plan so far and he expected to see continued bipartisan support for the effort.

Senate Republicans are considering adding additional aviation funds through a filibuster-proof reconciliation bill, a process that could begin as soon as this week with a floor “vote-a-rama” on a resolution to unlock that process. Cruz remarked that while reconciliation could be the vehicle used, additional aviation funds need to be “safety-focused.”.

According to recent reports, sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., noted after the lunch with Duffy and Bedford that he expects Congress will look at a package more in the $10 billion to $30 billion range.

In a recent development, for his part, Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., mentioned the airline industry itself should foot at least a portion of the bill, considering how much federal support the carriers have received over the years.

According to recent reports, “I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We give them unbelievable amounts of money,” Scott remarked, adding that he doesn’t like adding to the deficit and is “not big on government running things.”.

Duffy explained the need for the high price tag as the result of decades of pent-up demand that are now threatening major disruptions and safety risks to the traveling public.

Recent findings suggest that “This has never been done. To be clear, we are keeping planes safe in the sky, and we are switching out equipment that’s been a problem for decades,” he noted. “I and the president have decided we are going to lean in and fix it.”.

According to recent reports, he called the effort a “historic investment” reflecting the ways air travel has changed since much of the nation’s infrastructure was built — noting that the newest tower was constructed in 1969 and much of the software being used is from the 1990s. Still, Duffy remarked, on the current course of funding, it would take 300 years to replace every U.S. tower.

According to recent reports, “I'm not going to tell [Congress] how to do their work, but I'm telling everybody what we need,” Duffy noted. “And whether it's a party-line vote or if it's a bipartisan vote, I do think this is one moment in a very charged political environment — one moment where almost all Americans and bipartisan members of both bodies are kind of in agreement that we should lean in to do this.”.

Even as Duffy petitioned for additional funds Tuesday, he said that the “root cause” of the equipment instability that made the ground stop necessary is still unclear as investigators analyze the router that caused the problem.

A “routine switchover” from old copper wires to digital fiber in the telecommunications system “started to create issues in our network,” Duffy explained Tuesday.

Sources indicate that the telecommunications transition includes the conversion of thousands of routers to what are known as Juniper devices — a process being undertaken by contractor L3Harris Technologies. Duffy and Bedford explained that 68 other routers had been converted without incident prior to the problematic switchover Friday.

Bedford noted Tuesday that use of the router that officials have identified as the source of the system instability has been suspended “and we've disabled the ones that are out there.”.

Sources indicate that the decision to suspend use of the router followed an inquiry sent to the agency by Senate Commerce Committee Democrats a day prior. “With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation,” they wrote.

Bedford noted he was “highly confident” that similar problems wouldn’t erupt again. “Every element of this is going to be analyzed to see what we learn here and make sure that it doesn't get repeated,” he said.

David Jordan, Lia Chien and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

P&O Cruises has partnered with Harding+ and Bunnahabhain to offer guests at sea the Bunnahabhain 17-Year-Old Ruby Port Cask Finish, an exclusive Islay single malt.

The drink was selected by the P&O Cruises & Harding+ teams and bottled exclusively for guests.

Limited to just over 300 bottles, the Bunnahabhain release marks a first for both P&O Cruises and Bunnahabhain, the organization said in a press release.

Sources indicate that the exclusive release will be available across all seven P&O Cruises ships from early November. Onboard the Iona, the launch will take place through a Bunnahabhain pop-up activation across November and December.

Carnival UK and P&O Cruises president Paul Ludlow noted: “Creating memorable experiences for our guests is at the heart of everything we do and this exclusive partnership with Harding+ and Bunnahabhain is a great example of that.”.

“By working together to select and bottle a whisky available only on board our ships, we’re giving guests the opportunity to discover something genuinely unique, while bringing to life the sense of exploration and discovery that makes a holiday with P&O Cruises so special,” added Ludlow.

Lynsey Eades, head of global travel retail, CVH Spirits (Bunnahabhain Distillers), remarked: “We’re incredibly excited to bring this exclusive launch to life through our partnership with Bunnahabhain and Carnival UK.”.

“This marks an exciting first at sea for Bunnahabhain and is a fantastic example of what can be achieved through strong collaboration between Bunnahabhain, Carnival UK and Harding+,” added Eades.

Industry observers note that “Together, we’re focused on bringing distinctive brands and unique experiences to guests, and this launch reflects our shared ambition to create something truly special in the cruise retail environment. We look forward to building on this strong partnership and seeing the launch come to life.”.

According to the press release, the activation will be supported by dedicated in-store marketing materials, a whisky tasting masterclass and gifts with purchase on selected Bunnahabhain expressions, throughout the activation period.

Harding+ COO Linzi Walker added: “P&O Cruises brings its understanding of its guests, Bunnahabhain its exceptional whisky-making heritage and Harding+ our insight into what our guests want to discover and experience at sea, alongside our focus on creating distinctive onboard retail experiences.”.

“Together, we can offer something genuinely special that guests won’t find anywhere else,” added Walker.

Cristian Mungiu’s Latest Drama Fjord Plunges Into the Depths of Coastal Norway

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that on Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television demonstrates, and more.
  • Following in the footsteps of Anatomy of a Fall and Sentimental Value, Cristian Mungiu’s newly introduced film Fjord continues a recent trend of complex, critically acclaimed family dramas set against a gorgeous—if appropriately chilly—European backdrop.
  • It has been revealed that loosely based on a real court case, Fjord follows a devout evangelical Romanian man named Mihai (Sebastian Stan) and his Norwegian wife Lisbet (Renate Reinsve) who move to a remote fjord village in Norway with their five children.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that on Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television demonstrates, and more. This time, we take a look at Fjord.

Following in the footsteps of Anatomy of a Fall and Sentimental Value, Cristian Mungiu’s newly introduced film Fjord continues a recent trend of complex, critically acclaimed family dramas set against a gorgeous—if appropriately chilly—European backdrop. The Romanian New Wave director won his second Palme d’Or at this year’s Cannes Film Festival for the Norway-set film, which is also his first shot outside of his home country and Romania’s official selection for the best international feature category at the 2027 Oscars.

It has been revealed that loosely based on a real court case, Fjord follows a devout evangelical Romanian man named Mihai (Sebastian Stan) and his Norwegian wife Lisbet (Renate Reinsve) who move to a remote fjord village in Norway with their five children. Their conservative lifestyle soon puts them at odds with their progressive neighbors, and they find themselves in a custody battle after child abuse allegations surface, setting up a complicated debate between two opposing cultures and worldviews.

Cristian Mungiu’s latest film is based on a real-life court case.

According to recent reports, the film was shot over 36 days in spring 2025 in Western Norway’s Hjørundfjorden. The dramatic and mostly tourist-free fjord near the city of Ålesund cuts through the Sunnmøre Alps, with peaks rising up to 5,600 feet directly from the water.

In a recent development, for the family home, location scouts selected a tiny village called Stenes, comprising just a few rustic buildings scattered on the shores of the fjord’s Norangsfjorden arm. Nearby, they shot church scenes at a simple wooden structure in the town of Øye with school scenes taking place in Sæbø and courthouse scenes being filmed in the “massive city” of Ålesund.

Sources indicate that as the title of the film suggests, the fjord is more than just a mere setting—it’s a poetic space suffused with symbolic meaning for Mungiu. “I was attracted by this idea of a very secluded community where people can’t avoid finally talking to one another,” Mungiu says. “The fjord evokes for me this need for solidarity among people when confronted with extreme coldness and severe weather.”.

Mungiu sought to balance the epic scale of the fjord setting with the legal drama of the film.

Recent findings suggest that while audiences might expect the grandeur of a fjord to humble the people who live within it, in this movie, Mungiu instead uses the geographical formation to highlight their folly. “Normally, in front of nature’s force, people should become conscious of their fragility,” Mungiu states, “but too often their huge egos make them forget how mortal and insignificant they are, and they end up investing all their energy into imposing their point of view on others.”.

It has been revealed that the landscape worked particularly well within the context of Mungiu’s unique visual storytelling style: He conceives of each scene as a single shot, without cuts or close-ups, letting his characters move through expansive frames. As he describes it, “Every shot needs to be perfectly balanced in terms of light, interpretation, choreography, rhythm.” For this project, he imagined scenes that would call to mind the winter landscapes of Flemish Renaissance master Pieter Bruegel the Elder, who painted small human figures dwarfed by snowy scenery. The wide shots, Mungiu claims, “allow the majestic nature to feel a bit intimidating and menacing.”.

The winter landscapes in the film were inspired by the work of Flemish Renaissance painter Pieter Bruegel the Elder.

When it came time to select the perfect fjord, Mungiu was purely pragmatic. “I imagine scenes quite in detail when I write the screenplay and while scouting,” he explains. “I try to find locations as close as possible to what I’ve imagined.” He drew a “very precise sketch” for his location scout of what he was looking for: two neighboring houses at the end of a fjord, “with mountains and forests behind, quiet deep water in front, and a narrow road connecting them to the rest of the world—all this ideally covered in snow during wintertime.”.

His production team found a spot that looked just as he envisioned in Stenes, deep down the fjord and away from the coast, to maximize the potential for more snow. Then the hardest part started: convincing the homeowners to rent their properties out for the shoot.

“Once we started our scouting, we felt that we were visiting a form of paradise,” he states. “The light always comes from an angle, the air is pure, the colors are strong, the calm of the ocean is threatening, the snow on the peaks looks menacing.” Everything in the area, he continues, “is clean, organized, precise, logical, and functional.” Mungiu jokes, “For an OCD person like me, it was the perfect place.”.

Industry observers note that of course, the wildness of the fjord came with its own set of challenges, from avalanche warnings to a lack of consistent snow cover (they trucked in powder from the mountains). But Mungiu and his team tried to use these issues to their artistic advantage. On the first day of shooting, for instance, a major storm forced them to move production inside and shoot an emotionally complex scene. Inspired by the dramatic gusts, they hung an enormous Norwegian flag just outside the window to thrash and snap in the gale, “adding a visual element to the inner feelings of Lisbet in a very delicate moment for her as a character.”.

The primary gateway town for the fjord is Ålesund, a coastal city known for its abundant Art Nouveau architecture. While it’s only about 20 miles from Stenes as the crow flies, the journey takes about two hours of scenic driving and ferry crossings to get to the spots where the movie was shot.

Sebastian Stan as Mihai Gheorghiu, the devout evangelical main character who relocates his family to the titular Norwegian fjord.

If you want to see the fjord for yourself, an ideal lodging option is the lovely Hotel Union Øye, which opened early for the season to host the cast. Now a member of Relais & Châteaux, the gingerbread-like hotel debuted in 1891 and over the decades has hosted the likes of Henrik Ibsen, Arthur Conan Doyle, and Edvard Grieg, who composed music on the piano in the salon.

Recent findings suggest that it’s also possible to visit Hjørundfjorden on one of Norway’s most iconic journeys: a sailing with Hurtigruten, which is part pleasure cruise line, part local passenger ferry, and part cargo vessel for remote communities. In 2027, the line’s Coastal Express route, which hugs the coast from Bergen in the south to Kirkenes in the north, will visit Hjørundfjorden in May and September, while the Svalbard Line will make a stop at Sæbø in the fjord from May through September. (In the film’s Ålesund-set courtroom scenes, you can even see the ferry looming outside the windows.).

Havila Voyages, a family-run Hurtigruten competitor, also stops in Hjørundfjorden seasonally from September 1 to October 31; optional excursions include a scenic drive through the surrounding countryside and mountain valleys; an e-bike tour through the narrow Norangsdalen valley along the “Queen’s Route” (so named because it was supposedly visited by seven queens); or a guided hike to a mountain dairy farm, followed by a snack of a svele (crepe).

And if you can’t make it to Norway, Mungiu is presenting an exhibition of his photographs from scouting trips and the film’s production called Fjord. The Pictures at Latest York’s Romanian Cultural Institute in New York (through November 30). His images, all shot on a phone, depict the landscapes, people, architecture, and even weather that helped shape the film’s visual language.

MSC Foundation’s Coral Restoration Efforts Resume at Ocean Cay

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The MSC Foundation has resumed coral outplanting at Ocean Cay in The Bahamas, as ocean temperatures start to decline following a summer of marine heat stress.
  • The Foundation’s marine science team detected bleaching in fragments of one genotype of critically endangered staghorn coral (Acropora cervicornis), but, encouragingly, no visible signs of bleaching were observed in the critically endangered elkhorn coral (Acropora palmata).
  • Shade structures were installed over underwater nurseries to reduce exposure to intense sunlight and transferred some affected fragments to land-based nursery tanks at the Marine Conservation Center, where they are monitored while they recover.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The MSC Foundation has resumed coral outplanting at Ocean Cay in The Bahamas, as ocean temperatures start to decline following a summer of marine heat stress.

The Foundation’s marine science team detected bleaching in fragments of one genotype of critically endangered staghorn coral (Acropora cervicornis), but, encouragingly, no visible signs of bleaching were observed in the critically endangered elkhorn coral (Acropora palmata).

Shade structures were installed over underwater nurseries to reduce exposure to intense sunlight and transferred some affected fragments to land-based nursery tanks at the Marine Conservation Center, where they are monitored while they recover.

“As water temperatures decline, we are resuming outplanting while continuing to monitor coral health. Our priority is to protect vulnerable corals and better understand how different genotypes respond to repeated heat stress,” said Emeline Bouchet, marine program manager at the MSC Foundation.

“Every observation helps us refine our restoration methods. By tracking coral growth, recovery and survival, both in our nurseries and on surrounding reefs, we are building the scientific knowledge needed to make restoration more effective in a changing ocean.”.

According to data from the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Coral Reef Watch show, The Bahamas experienced significant accumulated marine heat stress during summer 2026, but satellite observations indicate that heat stress is easing in parts of The Bahamas since early November.

Although conditions are improving, continued monitoring remains crucial as severe marine heatwaves are forecasted in 2027.

Monitoring forms part of the Foundation’s long-term Super Coral Reefs Program, implemented at its Marine Conservation Center (MCC) on Ocean Cay.

The program focuses on identifying and propagating corals with promising stressor resistance and resilience characteristics, cultivating fragments in controlled land-based tanks and underwater nurseries, and outplanting them onto surrounding reefs.

In August, 32 nursery-grown fragments of elkhorn coral were outplanted on a reef near Browns Cay.

#214626. How the Antigravity 360 Drone Will Change Your Travels

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nomadicmatt ↗ Open Full Page

How the Antigravity 360 Drone Will Change Your Travels

📅 23 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1542 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nomadicmatt

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that drones are huge.
  • There’s lots of amazing brands out there but one that I think is super cool is the Antigravity A1.
  • I was sent one to use and want to share my experience and why I like this product so much.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that drones are huge. And, while there’s lots of restrictions around them, a lot of travelers take them on road because they produce some amazing sweeping aerial shots.

There’s lots of amazing brands out there but one that I think is super cool is the Antigravity A1. Released in late 2025, attempts to render the traditional gimbal obsolete for a vast segment of creators. By leveraging a dual-lens 360-degree capture system, the A1 records everything in every direction simultaneously. The result is a “fly now, frame later” experience that feels less like piloting a drone and more like directing a virtual camera in a pre-recorded digital environment.

I was sent one to use and want to share my experience and why I like this product so much.

What make’s Antigravity 360’s so special is the two lenses. Most drones feature a single lens that points forward. However, the A1 features two ultra-wide-angle lenses positioned on the top and bottom of the central fuselage that each captures a 200-degree field of view. When those images are combines, they overlap to create a seamless 360-degree sphere.

And, in the final exported footage, the drone itself is digitally removed, creating the illusion of a camera floating in mid-air with no visible means of support.

In a recent development, the sensors themselves are 1/1.28-inch CMOS units. While smaller than the 1-inch sensors found on some “Pro” level photography drones, they are massive compared to typical 360 action cameras. This allows for significantly better low-light performance and a higher dynamic range, capturing details in the highlights and shadows that would typically be lost in the harsh contrast of a midday sun.

Most countries require drones weighing 250 grams or more to be registered and subject to stricter flight rules. Antigravity clearly understood the importance of this threshold because they made the A1 to weigh exactly 249 grams with its standard battery meaning it’s not considered a commercial drone so you don’t have to register it.

And the drone feels remarkably sturdy. It utilizes a high-grade carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer that offers a better strength-to-weight ratio than the standard ABS plastic found in cheaper models. The folding mechanism is satisfyingly tactile, clicking into place with a precision that suggests long-term durability. When folded, the drone is roughly the size of a large smartphone, though about three times as thick.

According to recent reports, the Vision Goggles: These are sleek, lightweight, and feature dual 4K micro-OLED displays with a 120Hz refresh rate. The latency is nearly non-existent and they have integrated head tracking. Because the drone is recording in 360 degrees, you aren’t limited to seeing what is in front of the drone. When you turn your head to the left, the goggle feed pans to the left. If you look down, you see the ground passing beneath you. This provides a sense of presence and spatial awareness that is simply impossible with a traditional fixed-camera drone.

The drone uses a single-handed motion controller. You point the controller where you want to go and pull the trigger to accelerate. Tilt your wrist left to bank, or raise the nose of the controller to climb. It is an incredibly intuitive system that allows even a novice to fly through complex environments within minutes. For professional FPV pilots who prefer the precision of manual acrobatic flight, the A1 does support a traditional “Mode 2” stick controller, but the motion controls are so fluid that most people will likely never switch back.

Here’s a video of the drone in action:.

In a recent development, the marketing for the Antigravity 360 proudly displays “8K Resolution.” In a traditional camera, 8K means every pixel is packed into a 16:9 rectangle. In 360 video, those pixels are spread across a full sphere. When you “reframe” that 8K sphere into a standard flat video, you are looking at a “crop” of the total image.

According to recent reports, the color science is noticeably improved over previous 360 cameras. The A1 features a “Vivid” profile for those who want punchy, social-media-ready colors, and a 10-bit “Log” profile for professional editors who need to match the footage to other cameras in a color-grading suite. The stabilization, powered by Antigravity’s “FlowState” algorithms, is nothing short of miraculous. You can fly in 20mph winds, and the footage remains as steady as if the camera were on a tripod.

The “Antigravity Studio” app allows you to download footage wirelessly (at speeds up to 80MB/s) and reframe your video using your phone’s gyroscope. You simply watch the video and move your phone around to “film” the scene in real-time. The app also features “Auto-Frame,” an AI tool that identifies subjects and automatically generates a cut that keeps them in focus. For a solo creator, this effectively provides a virtual camera crew that never misses a shot.

Recent findings suggest that battery technology remains the bottleneck for all small drones. The A1’s standard Intelligent Flight Battery provides a theoretical 24 minutes of flight. In real-world conditions with moderate wind and constant recording, expect closer to 19 or 20 minutes.

While 20 minutes sounds short, the “work per minute” is much higher than a traditional drone. Because you don’t need to re-fly a path to get different angles, a single 20-minute flight can yield the same amount of usable footage as three flights with a Mavic. For those who need more time, the “Pro Battery” (which pushes the weight over 250g) offers a staggering 39 minutes of flight time, though it does compromise the drone’s agility slightly.

Recent findings suggest that in terms of flight dynamics, the A1 is a “cinewhoop” style flyer. It is stable and predictable rather than aggressive and twitchy. It has a top speed of roughly 36 mph, which is plenty for following bikes or cars, but it won’t keep up with a professional racing drone. The “Turtle Mode” is a life-saver; if you crash and end up upside down, the drone can flip itself over using its propellers, allowing you to take off again without a “walk of shame” to recover the aircraft.

The Antigravity 360 is a niche product that is rapidly becoming mainstream.

The Antigravity 360 (A1) is the most exciting drone I have tested. By removing the need for a gimbal and the stress of manual framing, it allows the pilot to focus on the one thing that truly matters: the story they are trying to tell.

While the image quality isn’t quite at the level of a high-end cinema drone, and the lenses are admittedly delicate, these are small prices to pay for the creative liberation the A1 provides. It bridges the gap between traditional cinematography and the immersive world of VR.

If you are a creator who is tired of the same old “drone shots” and want to push the boundaries of what is possible in the air, the Antigravity 360 is an essential addition to your toolkit.

Tech Report: The Best German Christmas Markets Are Straight Out of a Fairy Tale
