    Why A Part 103 Ultralight Needs No Pilot's License In The US & Weighs Under 254 Pounds

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1594 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that ethan is an aviation professional with a degree in Aviation Management with Flight from the Florida Institute of Technology.
    • It has been revealed that he right now holds a Restricted ATP and Commercial Multi‑Engine Pilot certificate and works in aviation supply chain and aircraft component repair.
    • A lifelong aviation enthusiast, Ethan spent countless hours at Raleigh–Durham International Airport’s observation deck studying air traffic and practicing amateur photography and videography.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that ethan is an aviation professional with a degree in Aviation Management with Flight from the Florida Institute of Technology. He previously wrote aviation and tourism features for Florida Tech’s student newspaper, The Crimson, where he developed a clear, reader‑focused reporting style. Aviation journalism has remained a consistent priority throughout his career.

    It has been revealed that he right now holds a Restricted ATP and Commercial Multi‑Engine Pilot certificate and works in aviation supply chain and aircraft component repair. Alongside his industry role, he is pursuing his Certified Flight Instructor rating and actively building flight experience.

    A lifelong aviation enthusiast, Ethan spent countless hours at Raleigh–Durham International Airport’s observation deck studying air traffic and practicing amateur photography and videography.

    Recent findings suggest that many people assume that flying any type of aircraft requires extensive training, a pilot certificate, medical approval, and federal registration. While that holds true for most types of licenses, such as a Certified Flight Instructor certificate (CFI) or Airline Transport Pilot (ATP), the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has long maintained a narrow exception that allows certain recreational flyers to take to the skies without obtaining a pilot license. The exception falls under FAA Part 103, a section of federal regulations governing ultralight vehicles and the strict limitations placed upon them.

    Recent findings suggest that while Part 103 is broadly described as allowing someone to fly without a license, the reality is more nuanced. The regulation applies only to a highly specific category of lightweight recreational aircraft that must meet strict performance, weight, and operating requirements. Understanding what qualifies under Part 103 helps explain where the FAA draws the line between recreational freedom and traditional pilot certification requirements.

    According to recent reports, yes, you can legally fly an aircraft in the United States without a pilot certificate, but only if the aircraft qualifies as an ultralight vehicle under FAA Part 103. These vehicles occupy a unique regulatory category that exempts operators from requirements including pilot licensing, aircraft registration, airworthiness certification, and medical certification. The exemption was created to support recreational flying while limiting risk through strict aircraft performance restrictions.

    Industry observers note that for powered ultralights, the FAA limits empty weight to 254 lb (115.2 kg), fuel capacity to five gallons (18.9 liters), maximum level-flight speed to 55 knots, and maximum power-off stall speed to 24 knots. Because these aircraft are intentionally small and limited in capability, the FAA regulates them differently than conventional airplanes.

    According to recent reports, the concept dates back decades, when regulators sought a framework that would allow simple recreational flying without imposing the full regulatory burden associated with general aviation aircraft. Rather than focusing on pilot certification, Part 103 controls risk by limiting what the aircraft can do. According to the FAA's regulations, qualifying ultralight vehicles are intended solely for sport and recreational purposes and are limited to carrying a single occupant.

    A common misconception is that any small aircraft can be flown without a license. In reality, FAA Part 103 sets detailed technical requirements an aircraft must meet to qualify as an ultralight vehicle. The term Ultralight is a specific category issued by the FAA for licensing and certification, such as airplane, rotorcraft, or glider for pilot ratings. While an FAA certificate typically prints the category and class, the lack of a true license requirement omits this display.

    Recent findings suggest that the most vital requirements involve weight, occupancy, fuel capacity, and performance. Powered Ultralights operate on the basis of minimal configurations of these variables. Ultralight aircraft should not be confused with Light Sport Aircraft, the next category up in the FAA's classification; they also have slightly different regulatory requirements, such as a higher speed limit of 250 knots and the ability to carry an additional passenger. These privileges come at the cost of training for a sport pilot certificate, among other requirements as outlined in 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart J, and 14 CFR Part 91.327.

    Maximum 5 gallons (18.9 liters).

    In a recent development, unpowered ultralights, such as many hang gliders, fall under a different weight limit. Under Part 103, these vehicles must weigh less than 155 pounds (70.3 kg) empty. By restricting both weight and performance, the FAA effectively prevents Part 103 aircraft from evolving into conventional airplanes that would normally require certification and pilot qualification.

    Recent findings suggest that although operators are exempt from licensing requirements, they are not exempt from federal aviation regulations. FAA Part 103 establishes operational limitations designed to protect both ultralight pilots and the public on the ground. Interestingly enough, Ultralight aircraft are not governed by either 14 CFR Part 61 or Part 91, which is the usual home for general aviation operation guidelines.

    Among the most key restrictions are where and when ultralights may fly. Operations are generally limited to daylight hours and must avoid congested areas, cities, towns, and open-air assemblies of people. The rules also restrict operations within controlled airspace (Class A, B, C, D, E, and most special use airspace) unless prior authorization has been obtained from air traffic control.

    These requirements show that the FAA's approach is not deregulation but targeted regulation. Operators may not need a pilot certificate, but they are still responsible for understanding airspace, weather conditions, and applicable operating restrictions before every flight. For many ultralight enthusiasts, voluntary training remains a common safety practice despite the absence of a licensing requirement.

    While FAA regulations do not require formal flight training for Part 103 operations, aviation organizations consistently encourage it. Groups such as the Experimental Aircraft Association (EAA) have long promoted structured training programs for ultralight pilots, emphasizing that regulatory exemptions do not eliminate the risks associated with flight.

    It has been revealed that the EAA's Ultralight Sourcebook notes that Part 103 provides significant operational freedom but also places responsibility squarely on the operator. Similarly, many flight instructors and aviation educators recommend dual instruction in two-seat trainers before attempting solo ultralight operations. Pilot Institute has also highlighted that, despite the absence of licensing requirements, knowledge of weather, aerodynamics, and operating limitations remains critical for safe flight. Industry recommendations reflect a broader understanding that flying skills and regulatory requirements are not necessarily the same thing. A pilot may legally operate a Part 103 vehicle without a certificate, but aviation organizations generally view training as one of the most effective safety measures available.

    Recent findings suggest that cost is another important variable. While flight training for a Private Pilot License (PPL) can range from $9,000 to $130,000, Ultralight aircraft operation has a less burdensome barrier to entry. Because no official license is required by the FAA, training costs alone are significantly lower. In general, however, ultralight aircraft are much less common in the general aviation landscape than, for instance, a Cessna 172. The good news is that outright ownership of ultralight aircraft is also more accessible. Aerocorner reports that the cheapest latest ultralight aircraft in 2026 is the Mini-Max 1103R, a single-seat wood-and-fabric kit that Mini-Max USA lists at $10,899.99 for the airframe. Also available is a finished, ready-to-fly example at about $22,500.

    It has been revealed that the same restrictions that make Part 103 accessible can also limit its practicality. Ultralight aircraft operation is the strictest modality of aviation under the FAA's jurisdiction. While the qualifications are generally among the most accessible to the public, that accessibility comes with significant compromises. Aircraft designed to remain under the FAA's weight and performance limits generally offer less range, lower speed, and reduced capability compared to certified airplanes.

    Recent findings suggest that weather sensitivity is another consideration. Because ultralights are lightweight and often have minimal protection from the elements, operating conditions that might be manageable for larger aircraft can present greater challenges. The single-seat requirement also prevents pilots from carrying passengers or instructors during normal operations. Under Part 103, ultralight vehicles must fly during daytime hours with visual reference to the surface and meet basic Visual Flight Rules (VFR) weather minimums for their prescribed airspace. Reference to published manufacturer minimums is also imperative, particularly with respect to wind.

    According to recent reports, prospective ultralight pilots should also remember that local airspace considerations still matter. Before operating any Part 103 vehicle, operators should ensure they understand applicable airspace restrictions and any authorization requirements that may apply near busy airports. In the United States, ultralight aircraft cannot fly over congested areas or crowds, and they cannot enter controlled airspace (Class A, B, C, D, or surface Class E) without prior Air Traffic Control (ATC) authorization. Advisory Circular AC-91-36D also suggests that ultralight pilots voluntarily remain above 2000 feet (609.6 meters) above ground level (AGL) wherever possible.

    Industry observers note that the short answer is yes: FAA Part 103 allows certain ultralight vehicles to be flown legally in the United States without a pilot certificate, aircraft registration, medical certification, or airworthiness approval. However, that freedom exists only because the FAA imposes strict restrictions on aircraft weight, speed, fuel capacity, occupancy, and operating conditions.

    Sources indicate that rather than creating a loophole in aviation regulation, Part 103 represents a carefully structured compromise. The FAA permits recreational flyers to avoid many traditional certification requirements while ensuring that the aircraft themselves remain limited in capability and risk exposure.

    For aviation enthusiasts, Part 103 continues to provide one of the most accessible entry points into personal flight. Yet the regulation's enduring message remains clear: while a license may not be required, safe operation still depends on knowledge, preparation, and respect for the limitations of both the aircraft and the environment in which it flies.

    • Recent findings suggest that senators voted 48-51 against adopting the Iran war powers resolution that the House previously adopted in mid-September that would direct the president to withdraw U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., seen here at the Capitol on June 17, mentioned additional war powers votes are under discussion for when Democrats control both chambers in the 120th Congress. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    In a recent development, the Senate rejected a resolution Thursday meant to rebuke President Donald Trump over the Iran war weeks after the midterm elections demonstrated the depth of public anger about the war and its effects on the U.S. economy.

    Recent findings suggest that senators voted 48-51 against adopting the Iran war powers resolution that the House previously adopted in mid-September that would direct the president to withdraw U.S. forces from the war.

    As they have previously with similar measures, GOP Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky broke with their party to support the resolution, while Democratic Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania broke with his party to oppose it. Departing GOP Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina and Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who have at times voted in support of similar measures, this time voted against the resolution.

    Even if the resolution was adopted in both chambers of Congress, it would be largely symbolic since, as a concurrent resolution, it would not go to the president for his signature.

    But the vote afforded senators the opportunity to register their complaints about the war for the first time since Democrats routed Republicans in the midterm elections.

    It also comes amid a larger debate within the Democratic Party on how best to fulfill their campaign promise of ending the war as they prepare to take control of Congress next year.

    Recent findings suggest that democrats have become increasingly interested in trying to cut off funding for the war rather than continuing to hold war powers votes. But they are divided on whether to demand an immediate end to funding in the next government funding bill in December or to wait until they take power in January.

    “When we have the gavels, we are contemplating other things, and we're actually contemplating things in connection with the CR discussion,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., told reporters Thursday in an apparent reference to the debate among Democrats.

    Recent findings suggest that as of Nov. 13, the war has cost at least $48.3 billion, up from $47 billion last month, the nominee to be Navy comptroller, Arthur Miller, told the Senate Armed Services Committee at his confirmation hearing Thursday.

    Recent findings suggest that as with previous estimates, the number Miller cited Thursday includes munitions, equipment replacement costs and operational costs but does not factor in the cost of damage to U.S. bases, which alone is likely to run in the billions.

    According to recent reports, last week, a trio of Senate Democrats unveiled legislation to prohibit funding for offensive military operations in Iran that they said they intend to introduce as an amendment to the next government funding bill, which Congress will need to pass to avoid a government shutdown after Dec. 11.

    Sources indicate that on Thursday as the Senate voted on the war powers resolution, Sens. Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., and Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., two of the sponsors of the proposed amendment, demanded it be included in the next funding bill.

    “We’ve already tried tool after tool to get the president to rein in this conflict. Nine months in, defunding the war is the only way to force Trump to end it,” Duckworth, who vowed to vote against any continuing resolution that doesn’t include the amendment, remarked at a news conference.

    Industry observers note that sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., unveiled his own proposed amendment Thursday to bar any future and previous funding from being used to “support directly or indirectly combat activities by United States personnel in or over Iran, or in Iranian territorial waters” unless specifically authorized by Congress.

    His legislation is modeled off of language Congress passed in 1973 to cut off funding for the Nixon administration’s bombing campaign in Cambodia, Bennet’s office said in a news release.

    “When we vote on short-term spending in the near future, we can fund the government and end this war. It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve,” Bennet said in a statement.

    Meanwhile, the House is likely to vote again on a war powers resolution before year’s end.

    It has been revealed that “Before the lame duck’s over, I hope to enforce a war powers resolution vote, and it’ll be a chance for Republicans to say whether they did or didn’t get the message on Nov. 3,” Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., stated Thursday in a brief interview, referring to the date of the elections.

    It has been revealed that as with previous resolutions, Massie’s would direct the president to remove U.S. military units from hostilities against Iran unless specifically authorized by Congress or needed to defend against an imminent attack.

    It has been revealed that the resolution was filed Nov. 10, and under the 1973 War Powers Resolution, Massie can force a vote 15 calendar days after its introduction.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, one of the most interesting transatlantic flights will be returning yet again in 2027.
    • In the summer of 2018, an interesting domestic transatlantic route rolled out — it operated seasonally once weekly.
    • It’s a self-governing territory of France, situated in the northwestern Atlantic Ocean, near Newfoundland and Labrador.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, one of the most interesting transatlantic flights will be returning yet again in 2027. Maybe this will be the year I finally get to try it, even if there’s no premium cabin angle!

    In the summer of 2018, an interesting domestic transatlantic route rolled out — it operated seasonally once weekly. Specifically, ASL Airlines operated a Boeing 737-700 that was marketed by Air Saint-Pierre between Paris (CDG) and Saint Pierre and Miquelon (FSP).

    What’s Saint Pierre and Miquelon? It’s a self-governing territory of France, situated in the northwestern Atlantic Ocean, near Newfoundland and Labrador. The islands cover an area of about 93 square miles, and have a population of just about 6,000 people.

    It has been revealed that the territory’s airline, Air Saint-Pierre, only has turboprops, which the carrier flies to places like Halifax (YHZ), Montreal (YUL), and St. John’s (YYT). Obviously these planes aren’t capable of operating across the Atlantic, so the airline leases a Boeing 737 for the once weekly flight.

    This was the first time ever that we saw a nonstop link between these territories and mainland France. There were some other things that made this route interesting:.

    Sources indicate that the route ended up returning in 2019, was then paused in 2020 and 2021 due to the pandemic, and then returned in 2022 through 2026. The route will now be returning yet again, for the 2027 season, so it sure seems like this is basically a permanent thing.

    The once weekly flight between Saint Pierre and Miquelon and Paris will be returning in 2027, between June 21 and September 6, 2027.

    According to recent reports, the route will once again be operated by an ASL Airlines France Boeing 737-700, and the flight will be marketed and sold by Air Saint-Pierre. The flight will operate westbound on Mondays and eastbound on Tuesdays, as follows:.

    Paris to Saint Pierre and Miquelon departing 4:00PM arriving 6:30PMSaint Pierre and Miquelon to Paris departing 10:30AM arriving 8:05PM.

    Sources indicate that the 2,664-mile flight is blocked at 6hr30min westbound and 5hr35min eastbound. As you can see, the plane sits on the ground in Saint Pierre for quite a while. This is so that the crew can get their rest and operate the flight back the next day, rather than making them stay there for over a week.

    In a recent development, I imagine the airline is able to get a decent deal on parking at the airport for 16 hours. 😉 It’s also interesting since this is an eastbound daytime transatlantic flight, which is fairly rare.

    If you want to book a seat on this flight, below is the pricing for travel in both directions, with fares starting at €660 one-way for standard adult fares.

    Recent findings suggest that as you can see, the fare difference just comes down to the age of the traveler, as well as the level of flexibility you’d like, with fares either being non-refundable and non-changeable, non-refundable but changeable for a fee, or refundable and changeable. The plane is in an all-economy configuration, as there’s no premium cabin.

    Recent findings suggest that air Saint-Pierre will be bringing back its flight between Saint Pierre and Paris in the summer of 2027, operated by ASL Airlines. This is an absolutely fascinating route, and it’s so cool to see that it was rolled out in the first place, and is sticking around.

    According to recent reports, while the link between Paris and this French territory is obvious, it’s still kind of awesome that such a small territory can support a flight like this. But I guess the downside was fairly limited, since the route was subsidized from the beginning. Personally I find this to be the most intriguing transatlantic route.

    • It has been revealed that southwest Airlines has several co-branded credit cards with Chase.
    • This is my in-depth Southwest Priority Card review, covering the card’s benefits.
    • Link: Learn more about the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that southwest Airlines has several co-branded credit cards with Chase. Of the three personal cards, my favorite one is the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card.

    This is my in-depth Southwest Priority Card review, covering the card’s benefits. I’ll also explain how despite this being the highest annual fee personal card in the portfolio, I still think it represents the best deal. Now is also a good time to consider applying for the card if you’re a fan of Southwest’s popular Companion Pass perk.

    Link: Learn more about the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card.

    Before I review the Southwest Priority Card benefits in detail, here’s a high-level look at everything you need to know about the card:.

    Here are my thoughts on the Southwest Priority Card’s main pros and cons:.

    Recent findings suggest that if you’re thinking about applying for the Southwest Priority Card, you’re probably most interested in the welcome bonus it’s at the moment offering, along with its annual fee and general eligibility rules for getting the card. So let’s dive into those. I’ll also explain a recent change to how Southwest cards factor into qualifying for the Companion Pass, which pertains to all cards, not just the Priority.

    The Southwest Priority Card is offering a limited time welcome bonus: Earn 90,000 bonus points after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. This is higher than the standard welcome offer for the card, and its minimum spending requirement should be easy for most spenders to meet.

    In a recent development, rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Rapid Rewards points to be worth 1.2 cents each. So, to me, the points from this welcome offer are worth $1,080.

    Recent findings suggest that chase and Southwest have some pretty strict rules when it comes to who is eligible for the card. The Southwest Priority Pass is not available to anyone who right now has a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card, or anyone who has received a welcome bonus on a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card in the past 24 months. However, you are eligible if you have a Southwest business credit card.

    This is in addition to Chase’s general application rules, including the 5/24 rule, whereby you typically won’t be approved for a Chase card if you’ve opened five or more fresh card accounts in the past 24 months. However, that’s not enforced consistently.

    It has been revealed that when it comes to credit scores, there’s not a consistent score that you need to get approved for the card, though I’d hope to have a score in the “excellent” range. That being stated, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected, as it’s one of only many factors that determines card eligibility.

    The Southwest Priority Card has a $229 annual fee. As a point of comparison, the other personal cards have annual fees of $99 and $149, so the annual fee on this card is a bit higher. However, as I’ll explain below, the benefits could justify the premium annual fee.

    The card also has no extra cost to add authorized people, so you can add those for $0 each, so that authorized user spending can help you rack up rewards.

    The Southwest Priority Card has no foreign transaction fees, so this could be a useful card for your spending abroad. This is a Visa as well, and Visas are accepted pretty widely around the globe.

    Another rule worth mentioning here involves how Southwest credit card welcome bonuses help you earn the Companion Pass, which lets you bring a companion with you on flights (both cash and award tickets) and pay just taxes and fees.

    Sources indicate that for a long time now, the points earned as part of Southwest credit card welcome bonuses have counted towards the 135,000 qualifying points needed to earn the Companion Pass. But starting soon, credit card welcome bonuses will no longer count toward qualification.

    You’ll need to apply for a card by December 2, 2026, for your welcome bonus to count toward the Companion Pass for a final time. So apply for the Priority Card sooner rather than later if you’re hoping to earn that perk with the help of credit card spending.

    Now is also your last chance to get an annual boost of 10,000 Companion Pass qualifying points as a Southwest credit card holder. Starting next year, instead of a boost of 10,000 TQPs for having a Southwest card, you’ll get 10,000 TQPs if your TQP balance is 130,000 by December 31, 2027. That would be enough to get you to Platinum status, which will include unlimited Companion Pass trips as a benefit.

    It has been revealed that this change eliminates the easiest way to earn this valuable benefit, and it’s not the only latest rule: referral bonuses, anniversary points, bonus points from spending, and partner spending won’t count toward the Companion Pass either. In fact, Southwest’s rolling the Companion Pass into its highest elite tier, Platinum, and requiring either 140,000 TQPs or 100 qualifying flights to earn it.

    Beyond the Southwest Priority Card airline benefits, a major draw is the card’s points earning on every purchase you make — plus how it can help you work toward Southwest elite status through earning Tier Qualifying Points.

    The Southwest Priority Card offers the following points for credit card spending:.

    Personally, I’d generally only put spending on the card if you’re going for A-List status and/or Companion Pass, because there are better cards for everyday spending otherwise. But still, those are some fairly solid bonus categories.

    As part of an overhaul of the Rapid Rewards program, Southwest is simplifying TQP earning on credit cards. Starting in 2027, every dollar spent on a co-branded Southwest credit card will earn you one TQP. In other words, $35K in spending would earn you Silver, $65K in spending would earn you Gold, and $140K in spending would earn you Platinum.

    This earning rate is the same across cards, so this isn’t specific to the Southwest Priority Card.

    I have a dedicated post that covers how to redeem Southwest Rapid Rewards points for maximum value, but let’s briefly look at how you can use the points you earn from the Southwest Priority Card.

    Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, meaning that the value you get from your points is tied to the cash cost of Southwest tickets. There are a few different levels, ranging from Basic tickets to Choice Extra fares, so the exact value can vary a bit.

    In a recent development, basic award fares tend to offer the best redemption value. You’ll also usually get the best value on international Southwest routes to destinations like Costa Rica and Aruba. I’ve been able to get about 2.0 cents per point on these redemptions.

    Starting in spring 2027, Southwest will add points earning and redemption opportunities with select airline partners, which should make your Rapid Rewards points more valuable for international travel. The planned partners include Icelandair, China Airlines, and Etihad Airways — I look forward to seeing how these add value to the program.

    In a recent development, one great thing about the Southwest Rapid Rewards program is that there are no change or cancellation fees, and rebooking a fare when the price drops gets you a refund equal to any difference in points. Just note that Basic fares can only be changed by upgrading to a higher fare bundle, so for a cheaper Basic award you’d cancel and rebook rather than change.

    As Southwest’s highest annual fee personal credit card, the Southwest Priority Card has the most benefits, including several that can improve your travel experience with the airline. Here are the card’s most notable ongoing perks.

    Southwest Priority Card holders can select a Preferred seat on Southwest at the time of booking for no extra charge. If Preferred seats aren’t available on your flight, you should be able to select a standard seat for free. Preferred seats are located near the front of the cabin, so having one usually means you’ll board and deplane faster.

    Recent findings suggest that preferred seats generally cost about $30 to $60 extra, and selecting free Preferred seats at booking is a perk of Southwest Silver elite status. If you don’t have status and you’re able to use this benefit, you could get real value even after just a few Southwest flights.

    In a recent development, the Southwest Priority Card also offers unlimited upgrades to extra legroom seats within 48 hours prior to departure. This perk applies to the main cardholder as well as up to eight additional passengers on the same reservation.

    It has been revealed that extra legroom seat prices vary by route, but they generally cost roughly $40 to $100. On a route where they’re at the higher end of this range and you have multiple companions on your reservation, you could even recoup the Priority Card’s annual fee through one trip alone.

    Keep in mind that complimentary extra legroom seats within 48 hours of departure is another benefit of Southwest Silver status. So if you have that level of status or higher already, you don’t need the Priority Card to enjoy this perk.

    The Southwest Priority Card gets the primary cardholder and up to eight additional passengers on the same reservation a first checked bag at no additional cost. Checked bags on Southwest cost $45 each way, so this can save you up to $90 roundtrip on checked bag fees per person.

    With even a couple of roundtrip flights per year, this benefit can offset the annual fee — and about five one-way checked bags per year could cover it as well.

    With the Southwest Priority Card, you’ll be able to board with Group 5, or earlier if you have elite status or a fare or seat type that qualifies you for an earlier boarding group.

    Southwest has eight total boarding groups, so while there are several ahead of Group 5, it’s better than boarding last. This benefit applies to the main cardholder and up to eight passengers on the same reservation.

    Recent findings suggest that on your Southwest Priority Card anniversary every year, you’ll receive 7,500 bonus Rapid Rewards points. Southwest Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and you can generally expect that you’ll need around 83 Rapid Rewards points for every dollar of airfare you book.

    In other words, 7,500 bonus points get you around $90 in Southwest airfare annually. That covers more than a third of the annual fee right there.

    If you pay with your Southwest Priority Card you can save 25% on inflight Wi-Fi and drink purchases. You’ll receive statement credits for the 25% within two billing cycles of your purchase (though usually much faster than that).

    The Southwest Priority Card offers a variety of travel & purchase protection benefits, including:.

    Of course, you’ll want to check the cardmember agreement for the full terms & conditions associated with these benefits.

    Even though the Southwest Priority Card has the highest annual fee of any personal Chase Southwest card, it might be worthy of consideration.

    Many people love flying Southwest for the ability to earn the Southwest Companion Pass, the lack of change fees and vouchers that don’t expire. For others, Southwest is just a practical airline to fly on occasion, given its massive route network. Regardless, there’s lots of value in having points and benefits on Southwest.

    It has been revealed that that mentioned, not everyone needs a Southwest credit card — and even among Southwest credit cards, there’s a cheaper option that could make more sense if you only fly the airline a few times a year. Let’s look at some alternatives and how they stack up.

    Industry observers note that first, here’s a look at how the Southwest Priority Card compares to the other two personal Southwest cards. Note that all three cards have the free checked bag benefit and Group 5 boarding, so I left that out of the comparison table here.

    The Southwest Rapid Rewards® Premier Credit Card (learn more) is one step down from the Southwest Priority Card, with a $149 annual fee and slightly pared-down perks. If you care about getting complimentary Preferred seat selection at the time of booking, the Priority Card is a better pick, since the Premier Card only offers this within 48 hours of departure.

    Other differences between the Priority and Premier cards include:.

    The Southwest Premier Card could be a decent alternative if you want a lower annual fee and don’t care about the lower earning rate on Southwest and caps on the other bonus categories.

    It has been revealed that there’s also the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card (learn more). This is the entry-level personal Southwest credit card, with a $99 annual fee. As you’d expect, it has the fewest benefits among the personal Southwest cards. Here’s a quick breakdown:.

    I think the Southwest Priority Card provides significantly more value than the Southwest Plus Card, so the higher annual fee could still be worth it.

    If you’re looking to complement your Southwest Priority Card with a Southwest business card, consider the incredible Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Performance Business Credit Card (learn more). This card has some nice perks, including:.

    Sources indicate that chase Ultimate Rewards is a transfer partner with Southwest Rapid Rewards, and points transfer at a 1:1 ratio. As a general rule of thumb, you’re going to earn points at a faster rate through Ultimate Rewards than through Rapid Rewards, not to mention that your points have a lot more flexibility.

    Should you earn Rapid Rewards points directly with a Southwest card, or with a Chase Ultimate Rewards card?

    For context, some of the best cards for earning Chase Ultimate Rewards points include the following:.

    On top of that, the following four no annual fee cards earn points that can be converted into Ultimate Rewards points at a 1:1 ratio in conjunction with one of the above cards:.

    When providing credit card advice, my answer to whether or not it makes sense to get a certain card is usually “it depends.” and this is the case as well with the Southwest Priority Card, especially given the latest changes to the Southwest Rapid Rewards program.

    If you fly Southwest several times a year and want a free checked bag and complimentary Preferred seat selection, not to mention complimentary extra legroom upgrades, this card can be well worth it. That’s especially true if you don’t have elite status with Southwest already, since it offers some of these same benefits.

    According to recent reports, if you’re interested in the Priority Card and also want the chance to earn the Companion Pass, consider applying sooner than later. Southwest credit card welcome bonuses will no longer count toward Companion Pass qualification in 2027, and this card’s 90,000-point welcome offer can get you a good chunk of the way there.

    • Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., during a press conference on Thursday.
    • Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., endorsed a bipartisan initiative Thursday to adopt newly introduced rules aimed at speeding up Senate procedures but stopped short of calling for abolishing the filibuster, laying down a marker on a key internal debate for Democrats as he positions himself to challenge Senate Minority Leader Charles E.
    • Sources indicate that van Hollen joined Sen.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore. looks on as Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., during a press conference on Thursday. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images).

    Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., endorsed a bipartisan initiative Thursday to adopt newly introduced rules aimed at speeding up Senate procedures but stopped short of calling for abolishing the filibuster, laying down a marker on a key internal debate for Democrats as he positions himself to challenge Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

    Sources indicate that van Hollen joined Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., at a press conference Thursday to express his support for a plan from Merkley and Sen. Steve Daines, R-Mont., to, among other changes, adopt a “talking filibuster,” requiring senators to continuously hold the floor if they seek to prevent a bill or nomination from moving forward.

    Van Hollen went further to say that while his personal view is that the filibuster itself is “anti-democratic,” changes beyond what Merkley and Daines are proposing are a matter for further discussion.

    It has been revealed that “I’m in favor of filibuster reform,” Van Hollen remarked. “How and when we do that is a matter for the caucus to decide.”.

    The filibuster, a Senate tactic that effectively requires a 60-vote threshold to advance most legislation, has long been the subject of calls for change or outright abolition from members of both parties.

    Other changes Merkley and Daines unveiled in October include eliminating cloture requirements for nominations and amendments, reducing post-cloture time for legislation, and introducing a upcoming suspension process modeled after the House rules to allow bills with broad support to move rapidly.

    Merkley actually held two separate press conferences Thursday on his filibuster proposal, one with his Montana Republican co-sponsor and then later with Van Hollen, whose bid to become majority leader he has endorsed.

    At the earlier appearance, Daines remarked that he thought the changes, if adopted, would “truly be a cultural change for the Senate” and lead to greater bipartisanship.

    “We believe these reforms are appropriate no matter who is in the majority, no matter what the election outcomes were,” Daines noted.

    Daines also reiterated his view that implementing any rules changes would require 67 votes from the full chamber.

    But Democrats have been debating whether to use their newly introduced majority in 2027 to change the rules on the first day of the session with 51 votes, or to eventually employ the so-called “nuclear option,” a series of procedural moves leading to a simple majority vote.

    According to recent reports, democrats used that tool in 2013 to lower the voting threshold for advancing some presidential nominations with a simple majority, rather than 60 votes. A Republican majority followed in 2017 by extending that change to include Supreme Court nominations, and again in 2019 to reduce the number of hours between a cloture and final confirmation vote.

    A spokesperson for Schumer declined to comment on Van Hollen’s endorsement of the Merkley-Daines plan.

    Schumer has remarked he remains confident in his bid to remain party leader.

    Van Hollen reiterated Thursday that his “momentum is growing,” after several senators-elect have thrown their support behind the Maryland Democrat.

    “I think people recognize that if we're going to deliver on the big things that the American voters stood up for and voted for, you can't just go back to business as usual and status quo,” Van Hollen stated.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Qantas is at the moment set to launch five new routes between January and October 2027. They include a new link announced on November 26, when this article was written, which will be operated by QantasLink. Of course, compared to some of the other entries, it might not seem particularly noteworthy, but it is in its own right.

    In a recent development, as the article only focuses on 2027, the upcoming link from Sydney to Las Vegas, which will begin on December 29, is not included. Qantas will serve this market six times weekly using the Boeing 787-9. It'll be the first time that scheduled flights have existed, although charter services operated in the past.

    Obviously, a lot of the attention is on the much-discussed nonstop service from Sydney to London Heathrow, which will deploy the Airbus A350-1000ULR. The maximum block time is expected to be around 21 hours.

    It has been revealed that reflecting the highly prestigious nature of the route, AeroRoutes highlights that it'll use QF1/QF2, which is right now on Qantas' one-stop operation from Sydney to Heathrow via Singapore. The stopping service will then use QF5/QF6. Those numbers are currently on Sydney-Perth-Rome, which will become QF105/QF106.

    Recent findings suggest that 3 weekly QantasLink Dash 8-Q400 (Sunstate). See the next section.

    Industry observers note that 4 weekly QantasLink E190 (Alliance). Jetstar also operates.

    According to recent reports, 4 weekly QantasLink E190 (Alliance). Jetstar also operates.

    3 weekly 787-9. Qantas will now have 3 routes to South Africa. It'll be Cape Town's longest nonstop service in the Southern Hemisphere.

    The so-called Project Sunrise, and everything related to it, has been discussed in detail on many occasions. Tickets are meant to go on sale in February.

    In a recent development, theoretically, the nonstop operation to Heathrow will cover 9,100+ nautical miles (16,853+ km) each way. However, this is before adjusting the distance because of detours for closed airspace and chasing tailwinds and lower airspace costs. It'll cover more distance than that. Still, even before the alteration, it'd exceed the length of what is right now number one, Singapore Airlines to Fresh York JFK, by around 11%.

    Recent findings suggest that questions might be raised about the appeal of the upcoming nonstop service from Albury to the popular Gold Coast, which will have a maximum block time of two hours and 20 minutes on the Q400. However, QantasLink will be the third airline to attempt it since 2017.

    Cirium Diio data shows that the now-defunct JetGo flew in 2017/2018 using the Embraer ERJ135 and ERJ140. The now-defunct carrier Bonza followed in 2023/2024 using the Boeing 737 MAX 8. Bonza primarily focused on unserved markets, whether without head-to-head competition or brand-new.

    It has been revealed that like low-cost carriers elsewhere, Bonza used its higher-capacity equipment with much lower seat-mile costs to offer much more attractive fares, compounded by flying nonstop rather than connecting on the way. The lower fares were entirely to drive demand and therefore to grow the market's traffic.

    Sources indicate that booking data highlights that Albury-Gold Coast passengers increased by nearly 400% to over 23,000 in a year after the airline's entry. Of course, demand stimulation from the lower fares depressed the yields, but that always happens with LCCs. It is unclear if Bonza's fares fell by more or less than the traffic growth. It is unknown what the average fare was to achieve an approximate 80% load factor.

    In a recent development, qantasLink's operation will be radically different. It'll deploy the 76-seat Q400 rather than the 189-seat MAX 8, reducing round-trip weekly seats for sale from 1,134 to just 456. It'll not have to discount anywhere near as dramatically. That's just as well, as its much higher costs wouldn't let it, at least not sustainably. That's why its minimum round-trip fare is about USD$344 (AU$518). By only flying at more popular times of the year, rather than for weeks at a time and having to discount more, yields will not be depressed.

    QantasLink's fresh route to the Gold Coast will cover 579 nautical miles (1,072 km) each way. However, if statute miles are used instead, it'll be 666 miles, the so-called number of the beast. Schedule analysis suggests that only 11 routes globally will have this great circle distance when the Q400 service lifts off in March.

    It will be Albury's second-longest turboprop-driven scheduled link in nearly three years. QantasLink had operated the Q400 to Brisbane between July 2021 and May 2024, but that route has switched to the 96-seat E190 (other capacities operate occasionally). More seats contributed to the route's frequency falling to daily, down from the record high of two daily flights with the Q400.

    • Back in my late teens and early 20s, I was all for booking the cheapest ticket to a place I’d never heard of, just because I could.
    • Recent findings suggest that that remarked, I still do still love to find a bargain, and can spend hours researching the best value option even when booking the simplest of itineraries.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that love them or hate them, low-cost airlines dominate the skies in some parts of the world. Nowhere is that more true than in Europe, home to Ryanair, the largest low-cost airline in the world (per 2025 passenger numbers).

    Back in my late teens and early 20s, I was all for booking the cheapest ticket to a place I’d never heard of, just because I could.

    Recent findings suggest that that remarked, I still do still love to find a bargain, and can spend hours researching the best value option even when booking the simplest of itineraries. The buck stops, however, at Ryanair. My last flight was in 2023, and despite nothing glaringly awful happening, I vowed it would be the last.

    Part of the low-cost airline business model is choosing airports far from the cities they serve, since landing fees are often cheaper. One of the best examples of this is Frankfurt Hahn (HHN), located about 80 miles from Frankfurt am Main — the city the airport’s named after.

    In a recent development, after a quick check on the Uber app, a one-way Uber ride would likely cost around $180. A more wallet-friendly alternative would be this €24 bus. The journey time would likely be longer than the flight itself….

    Even Ryanair’s largest base at London Stansted (STN) is around 40 miles from London, and requires a relatively expensive train or lengthy bus journey to the city.

    Sources indicate that this is the part I hate the most about Ryanair. They are so stingy that they built their planes with built-in steps at the front boarding door so they don’t have to pay for air bridges. Whether it’s a sizzling 110+ degrees in the middle of the day in Seville, or deep in the minuses at Rovaniemi in Finland (the gateway to Lapland and Ryanair’s northernmost airport), you’ll have to brace the elements while boarding and deplaning.

    Recent findings suggest that getting a deal on a flight departing at daft o’clock in the morning isn’t limited to just Ryanair or low-cost airlines. Who would ever want to set an alarm before 6 a.m.? However, Ryanair can charge such a premium to fly at a respectable time of day, that its fares end up almost the same as flag carriers.

    The screenshot below is a great example. British Airways’ one-way fares of 88 pounds from Heathrow (LHR) are over twice as much as two of Ryanair’s options from Stansted to Berlin.

    However, Ryanair charges £74 for its midday departure (without a cabin bag). Compare that to BA’s 1:20 p.m. departure for £88 including a cabin bag; it’s a wonder why anyone would even consider Ryanair’s option if they needed to fly in the middle of the day.

    Recent findings suggest that ultimately, airline preference is very subjective, and I know there are some die-hard Ryanair fans who won’t hear a bad word remarked about the airline. In its defense, if you’re heading somewhere off the beaten track, you can usually rely on Ryanair to get you as close as possible.

    Personally, I’d rather enjoy status benefits (and earn miles and status-earning points) by flying a legacy carrier like Air France-KLM, British Airways, or Lufthansa to the closest airport, then figure out ground transportation the rest of the way.

    Where do you stand on flying Ryanair?

    Newly introduced FAA Rule For Planes Lining Up On Runways May Cause Delays

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1057 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has just added some newly introduced restrictions to how air traffic controllers can clear aircraft to “line up and wait” on the runway, in anticipation of takeoff clearance.
    • In a recent development, as of today (November 24, 2026), the FAA has introduced a fresh rule regarding how aircraft can be cleared onto runways at airports.
    • To give an example, sometimes a plane will be cleared for takeoff, and then a bit of separation is required until the next plane can depart.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has just added some newly introduced restrictions to how air traffic controllers can clear aircraft to “line up and wait” on the runway, in anticipation of takeoff clearance. This is intended to add an extra safety buffer, but to quote an airline pilot on an ATC frequency, “that’s probably going to cause some delays, that’s for sure.”.

    In a recent development, as of today (November 24, 2026), the FAA has introduced a fresh rule regarding how aircraft can be cleared onto runways at airports. Air traffic controllers want to utilize runways as efficiently as possible for both takeoffs and landings, and that often involves having planes line up on the runway and wait, in anticipation of takeoff clearance.

    To give an example, sometimes a plane will be cleared for takeoff, and then a bit of separation is required until the next plane can depart. In those situations, it’s common for the air traffic controller to clear that next plane to “line up and wait.”.

    Industry observers note that the idea is that the plane then has clearance to enter the runway, and then await further takeoff clearance. After all, it might take 30 seconds or so for a plane to taxi from the hold short point of the runway, to getting into position on the runway.

    Under the new FAA rules, air traffic controllers will only be allowed to clear pilots to “line up and wait” in situations where there’s a dedicated supervisor or controller-in-charge who can’t perform other duties while these operations are underway. In the past this was a recommendation, but now this is a rule.

    It has been revealed that given constant air traffic control staffing shortages, this could actually impact operations a good percentage of the time. Here’s how the reason for this policy change is described:.

    In a recent development, the core purpose of this change is to elevate the safety standard for Line Up and Wait (LUAW) operations by removing ambiguity in staffing requirements. By upgrading the guidance from “should” (a recommendation) to “must” (a mandatory requirement), the FAA ensures that the personnel providing watch supervision (OS/CIC) are fully dedicated to overseeing the safety of the operation without the distraction of simultaneously managing other operational tasks.

    I can appreciate the concept behind this, which is to improve safety. After all, we have air traffic controllers who are spread too thin, and all too often, they get a bit distracted due to the volume of things they have to deal with. That has definitely been a contributing factor to many accidents and incidents over the years.

    I do find the timing of this being introduced to be interesting, as it comes during one of the busiest travel periods of the year. I don’t think this will actually lead to any major complications, and for that matter, safety shouldn’t be compromised just because flights are busy.

    If you’re an observant passenger who is always looking out the window and is on Flightradar24, you may notice this policy in practice, for situations where you feel like the plane should already be lining up on the runway, but isn’t.

    I can’t imagine this policy change will lead to any major delays on a widespread basis, but then again, given how at capacity many airports are, even a little change can make a significant difference. Below you can hear some talk between an air traffic controller at Albuquerque Airport (ABQ) and a Southwest pilot, where they’re discussing the change. As you can hear, the pilot indicates “that’s probably going to cause some delays, that’s for sure.”.

    A upcoming FAA runway safety requirement takes effect across the United States tomorrow, November 24, and an air traffic controller in Albuquerque is already warning pilots about possible delays.The change requires airports to have a dedicated supervisor on duty before controllers… pic.twitter.com/zxXariHNAy.

    According to recent reports, while the FAA is making changes intended to improve safety, how about also requiring air traffic controllers in the United States to start using standard phraseology, like everywhere else in the world? 😉.

    As of today, the FAA has added a upcoming restriction on planes being able to line up on runways. A “line up and wait” procedure is pretty standard, but will now only be allowed in situations where the air traffic controller is only focused on one thing. Given how short staffed air traffic control often is, this could have some implications.

    I don’t think this will meaningfully slow things down on a national level, but for airports that make the most of every second to get planes in and out, it could definitely have implications.
